```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
set.seed(1989)
bayside_quizzes <- expand_grid(
  student = c("Zack", "Kelly", "Slater", "Jessie", "Lisa", "Screech"),
  semester = c("Fall 1990", "Spring 1991"),
  subject = c("Biology", "History"),
  quiz = 1:10) |>
  mutate(
    student = factor(student, levels = unique(student)),
    avg_score = case_when(
      student == "Zack" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 70, 80),
      student == "Kelly" ~ 82,
      student == "Slater" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 72, 78),
      student == "Jessie" ~ 91,
      student == "Lisa" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 84, 81),
      student == "Screech" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 93, 95)),
    score = round(pmin(100, rnorm(n(), mean = avg_score, sd = 8))))
bayside_slope <- bayside_quizzes |>
  group_by(semester, student) |>
  summarise(avg_score = mean(score)) |>
  ungroup()
labs_slope <- labs(
        title = "Bayside High quizzes",
        caption = "Simulated data",
        subtitle = "Fall 1990 & Spring 1991",
        x = "Semester", y = "Average quiz score",
        color = "Student")

ggp2_slope <- ggplot(data = bayside_slope,
    mapping = aes(x = semester,
                  y = avg_score,
              group = student)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = student), linewidth = 2,
      show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(color = student), size = 4) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top")

ggp2_slope +
    labs_slope
```

## Description

Slope graphs show changes in a numeric value (displayed on the `y` axis) typically over two points in time (along the `x` axis). The values for each group or unit of measurement are connected by lines, and any differences between the two time points are represented by the slope of the lines (hence the name, 'slope chart').

We can build slope graphs in `ggplot2` using the `geom_line()` and `geom_point()` functions.

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Install packages.
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for data manipulation
library(tidyr) # for expand_grid()
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

Mr. Belding's Bayside High gave us six students with very different relationships to homework: Zack scheming his way out of it, Screech and Jessie acing everything, and Slater and Kelly somewhere in between. We'll simulate ten biology quizzes and ten history quizzes for each student in the fall of 1990 and the spring of 1991. Each student gets an average score for each semester (`avg_score`). Zack and Slater improve in the spring, Lisa slips a little, and Kelly and Jessie stay exactly the same. `rnorm()` draws each quiz score around those averages, and `pmin()` caps the scores at 100. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same `r nrow(bayside_quizzes)` quizzes every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1989)
bayside_quizzes <- expand_grid(
  student = c("Zack", "Kelly", "Slater", "Jessie", "Lisa", "Screech"),
  semester = c("Fall 1990", "Spring 1991"),
  subject = c("Biology", "History"),
  quiz = 1:10) |>
  mutate(
    student = factor(student, levels = unique(student)),
    avg_score = case_when(
      student == "Zack" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 70, 80),
      student == "Kelly" ~ 82,
      student == "Slater" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 72, 78),
      student == "Jessie" ~ 91,
      student == "Lisa" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 84, 81),
      student == "Screech" ~ if_else(semester == "Fall 1990", 93, 95)),
    score = round(pmin(100, rnorm(n(), mean = avg_score, sd = 8))))
glimpse(bayside_quizzes)
```
:::

A slope graph needs one value per student per semester, so we'll average the 20 quizzes in each semester and store the results in `bayside_slope`.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_bayside_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| message: false
bayside_slope <- bayside_quizzes |>
  group_by(semester, student) |>
  summarise(avg_score = mean(score)) |>
  ungroup()
glimpse(bayside_slope)
```
:::

## Distribution

The slope of each line is the difference between two averages. Averages are much steadier than single quiz scores, but they're not perfectly steady, so a slope graph can show a small rise or fall even when nothing changed. Below we'll move from the quizzes, to a picture, to the formula, and work out how big a slope needs to be before we take it seriously.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with Zack's first five biology quizzes from the fall.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
bayside_quizzes |>
  filter(student == "Zack", semester == "Fall 1990") |>
  select(subject, quiz, score) |>
  head(5)
```
:::

Single quizzes bounce around by close to ten points. Below we compare each student's fall and spring averages (`change`) with the change we built into the simulation (`true_change`).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
slope_changes <- bayside_quizzes |>
  group_by(student, semester) |>
  summarise(avg = mean(score), truth = first(avg_score),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = semester, values_from = c(avg, truth)) |>
  mutate(change = `avg_Spring 1991` - `avg_Fall 1990`,
         true_change = `truth_Spring 1991` - `truth_Fall 1990`) |>
  select(student, change, true_change)
slope_changes
```
:::

Zack's and Slater's averages went up, just as they should. But Kelly's average dropped by about `r abs(round(slope_changes$change[slope_changes$student == "Kelly"], 1))` points, even though her true average didn't change at all.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The graph below shows every quiz for Zack and Kelly as a faded point, with the slope graph lines drawn through their semester averages. Zack's cloud of points shifts up in the spring. Kelly's two clouds sit in about the same place, and her line slopes down only because the spring quizzes happened to land a little lower.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
zack_kelly <- bayside_quizzes |>
  filter(student %in% c("Zack", "Kelly"))
ggplot(zack_kelly, aes(x = semester, y = score, color = student)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, alpha = 1 / 3, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = student), fun = mean, geom = "line",
               linewidth = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Quiz score", color = "Student")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Each quiz score is a draw from a [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) centered on the student's average for that semester (and capped at 100):

$$
\text{score} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{\text{student, semester}}, \; \sigma = 8)
$$

An average of $n = 20$ quizzes has a standard deviation of $\sigma / \sqrt{n} = 8 / \sqrt{20} \approx 1.8$ points (the [standard error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_error)). A slope is the difference between two of these averages, so its standard deviation is $\sqrt{1.8^2 + 1.8^2} \approx 2.5$ points. About 95% of slopes land within two standard deviations (about 5 points) of the true change. Kelly's drop is inside that range, while Zack's and Slater's gains are large enough to stand out. Try changing `quiz = 1:10` to `quiz = 1:40` and the noise in every slope is cut in half.

## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

  - Create labels with `labs()`

  - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

  - Map `semester` to the `x`, `avg_score` to `y`, and `student` to `group`

  - Add a `geom_line()` layer, mapping `student` to `color`, and setting the `linewidth` to `2`

  - Add a `geom_point()` layer, mapping `color` to `student`, and setting `size` to `4`

  - We'll move the `x` axis to the `"top"` of the graph with `scale_x_discrete()`

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_slope <- labs(
        title = "Bayside High quizzes",
        caption = "Simulated data",
        subtitle = "Fall 1990 & Spring 1991",
        x = "Semester", y = "Average quiz score",
        color = "Student")

ggp2_slope <- ggplot(data = bayside_slope,
    mapping = aes(x = semester,
                y = avg_score,
                group = student)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = student),
                linewidth = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(color = student),
                size = 4) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top")

ggp2_slope +
    labs_slope
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_slope
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_slope <- labs(
        title = "Bayside High quizzes",
        caption = "Simulated data",
        subtitle = "Fall 1990 & Spring 1991",
        x = "Semester", y = "Average quiz score",
        color = "Student")

ggp2_slope <- ggplot(data = bayside_slope,
    mapping = aes(x = semester,
                y = avg_score,
                group = student)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = student),
                linewidth = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(color = student),
                size = 4) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top")

ggp2_slope +
    labs_slope
```

## More info

We can also use faceting with slope graphs to add a third categorical variable.

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

We'll use the `bayside_quizzes` data again, but this time we group it by `semester`, `student`, and `subject`.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_grp_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| message: false
bayside_grp_slope <- bayside_quizzes |>
    group_by(semester, student, subject) |>
    summarise(avg_score = mean(score)) |>
    ungroup()
glimpse(bayside_grp_slope)
```

:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

  - Create labels with `labs()`

  - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

  - Map `semester` to the `x`, `avg_score` to `y`, and `student` to `group`

  - Add a `geom_line()` layer, mapping `student` to `color`, and setting the `linewidth` to `2`

  - Add a `geom_point()` layer, mapping `color` to `student`, and setting `size` to `4`

  - We'll move the `x` axis to the `"top"` of the graph with `scale_x_discrete()`

  - We'll duplicate the `y` axis with `sec.axis`, setting `dup_axis()` to the same `name` of the previous `y` label.

  - Finally, we facet the graph by `subject`, adjust the `size` of the text, and move the legend to the `"bottom"` of the graph.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_grp_slope
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.8
labs_grp_slope <- labs(
    title = "Bayside High quizzes",
    caption = "Simulated data",
    subtitle = "Fall 1990 & Spring 1991, by subject",
    x = "",
    color = "Student")

ggp2_grp_slope <- ggplot(data = bayside_grp_slope,
    mapping = aes(x = semester,
        y = avg_score,
        group = student)) +
    geom_line(aes(color = student),
        linewidth = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_point(aes(color = student),
        size = 4) +
    scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Average quiz score",
        sec.axis = dup_axis(name = "Average quiz score")) +
    facet_wrap(. ~ subject,
        ncol = 2) +
    theme(
        legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 10))

ggp2_grp_slope +
    labs_grp_slope
```
:::

Each subject average is built from only ten quizzes, so these slopes are noisier than the ones above (their standard deviation is about $\sqrt{2} \times 8 / \sqrt{10} \approx 3.6$ points). That's why Jessie's history line climbs while her biology line falls, even though her true average is the same in both semesters.
